speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: I will speak first on MHA's proposals, which achieve three objectives: firstly, to raise the penalties for some offences; secondly, to implement a theory test for the use of power-assisted bicycles (PABs) on roads; and thirdly, to enhance Traffic Police's operational efficiency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Dr Amy Khor, Senior Minister of State, will cover MOT's proposals to strengthen the land transport system, namely in the areas of autonomous vehicle trials, re-imposition of vehicle taxes and security searches of commuters using our public transport system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Our roads have become safer over the years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Traffic Police (TP) and the Land Transport Authority (LTA) have taken steps to improve road safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: First, TP stepped up public education efforts to get motorists to drive safely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: TP also conducts targeted public education for vulnerable road users, such as motorcyclists and elderly pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Second, TP also stepped up enforcement and expanded its enforcement camera network to improve detection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: In 2020, TP installed 12 more red light cameras.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: There are now close to 300 traffic enforcement cameras deployed to detect and deter speeding and red light running.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Third, raising penalties to deter irresponsible driving behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: In 2019, TP increased the amount of composition sums it offers for all traffic offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: The maximum jail terms and fines for serious traffic offences, such as dangerous driving and driving under influence, were also raised in the 2019 Road Traffic (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Fourth, LTA has installed infrastructure to make our roads safer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This includes School Zones and Silver Zones with lower speed limits and features to slow traffic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Road safety is a shared responsibility between drivers of motor vehicles, users of active mobility devices and pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Notwithstanding that our roads have become safer, we have identified a few other areas where road safety can be improved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: During these trials, racers far exceed the speed limit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: They also exhibit other dangerous behaviours, such as swerving in and out of lanes suddenly and without warning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: In December 2018, Police arrested five drivers for their suspected involvement in a case of dangerous driving and illegal racing along Lim Chu Kang Road.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: They raced at speeds averaging at least 110 kilometre per hour along a stretch of road which has a speed limit of only 70 kilometre per hour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: They were racing while there were other users on the roads.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: The consequences of an accident between them and these other innocent road users could have been devastating.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: From 2015 to 2017, 10 persons were convicted of this offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This is a stark increase compared to the previous three years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This aligns the penalties for illegal speed trials with those for offences of similar severity, such as dangerous driving endangering life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: That said, we recognise that offenders taking part in speed trials do not necessarily use their own vehicles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: For vehicles used in illegal speed trials, the Court is required to order the vehicle to be forfeited under section 117 of the Road Traffic Act or RTA, if the Public Prosecutor makes a written application for forfeiture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Clause 23 amends the forfeiture regime so that forfeiture is not automatic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Under the amended section 117, the Court need not make an order for the forfeiture of the vehicle if the Court is satisfied that: firstly, the person who committed the illegal speed trial offence was not the owner of the vehicle; and secondly, the person had used the vehicle without the owner's consent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This is fairer and better in line with other egregious RTA offences, such as dangerous driving causing death, where vehicle forfeiture is not mandatory.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Next are offences relating to protective helmets worn by motorcyclists and pillion riders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Helmets are a key safety feature for motorcyclists and pillion riders, just like seatbelts for drivers and passengers in cars.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Currently, it is an offence for pillion riders not to wear an approved helmet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: There is no present duty on the motorcyclist to see to this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Clause 19 will now make it an offence for the motorcyclist who fails to ensure that his or her pillion rider wears an approved helmet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This mirrors the duty that we place on drivers of other motor vehicles like cars to ensure that their passengers are wearing seat belts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Clause 19 further raises the maximum jail terms and fines for the existing offence of importing or selling unapproved helmet models.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: They will be aligned with the penalties for not wearing approved helmets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Next, the Bill also deals with individuals who obstruct, prevent or defeat the course of justice in road traffic incidents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: A vehicle owner has an obligation to provide information about the offending motorist when the owner's vehicle has been detected to be involved in an offence under the RTA or any of its rules.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: TP has encountered cases where the owner and offender-driver collude with another person to falsely declare to TP that another person was instead driving at the time of the commission of the offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Individuals involved in such schemes deserve to be more severely punished.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: For the owner or offender-driver who causes or permits to provide false or misleading information; or intentionally alter, suppress or destroy information that identifies the offender-driver.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This more appropriately reflects the severity of the offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Under existing law, the Courts can disqualify a motorist from driving if the motorist commits certain Penal Code offences in the context of a road rage situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Examples of such offences include voluntarily causing hurt and causing death by a rash or negligent act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This is because there are offences that were previously not in the list, but may be committed in a road rage situation, such as criminal intimidation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This approach gives the Courts greater discretion to impose disqualification in appropriate cases to better punish and deter road rage behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: I will now speak about the introduction of a theory test for the use of power-assisted bicycles, or PABs, on roads.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: The Active Mobility (Amendment) Bill was passed by Parliament on 4 February 2020 to require riders of personal mobility devices and PABs to pass a theory test before they can ride on public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: As PABs are allowed on both public paths and roads, it is only logical that we need to require PAB riders to pass a theory test before they can ride on roads.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: I highlight two main aspects of the amendments and how we intend to operationalise them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: PAB riders will only be required to undergo a single theory test before they can ride on either public paths or roads.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This theory test will be administered by LTA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: The theory test handbook can be found on LTA's website.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: More details of the test will be released in June.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: The theory test will comprise modules on both path and road safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: It will educate PAB riders on active mobility rules, road traffic regulations, the code of conduct and safe riding behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Under the new section 47K, it will also be an offence to employ or intentionally or negligently allow a rider to ride a PAB on a road if the rider has not passed the theory test.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This mirrors existing offences in the Active Mobility Act for the usage of PABs on shared paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: I will now move on to the third objective of the Bill, which is to enhance TP's operational efficiency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: First, to improve detection of traffic offenders, clause 20 introduces more reporting requirements for companies that own vehicles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: When a company's vehicle is detected to be used in a traffic offence and the motorist is unidentified, TP relies on the company owner to provide information to identify the motorist.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Some companies only get back to TP after being issued with numerous reminders while others do not get back to TP at all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This hampers TP's ability to take to task motorists who commit traffic offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: To ensure that companies provide TP with information to identify offender-motorists in a timely manner, section 81 is proposed to be amended to require companies to designate a "responsible officer" to see to the timely reporting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: For companies, the responsible officer will be someone holding the post of chairperson, managing director or company secretary, or any position that is analogous to these offices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: The responsible officer will have the duty to ensure that the company keeps proper records of motorists who use the company's vehicles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: If the company fails to provide information to TP to identify the motorist who had used the company's vehicle, the responsible officer may be held personally liable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This approach will help to ensure that records are properly kept and the company promptly provides the necessary information to TP.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: We will increase the period for which companies are required to keep records of the motorists who drive their vehicles from six months to one year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Some cases are highly complex and require extensive investigations, such as those involving multiple parties or where video footage is not readily available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Next, we will streamline the process of empowering TP officers to cancel notices to attend Court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Today, to empower a TP officer to cancel an accused's notice to attend Court, Police must first publish the TP officer's name in the Gazette.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This is cumbersome and hampers operational efficiency as the list will need to be updated whenever there is staff movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Clause 26 removes the requirement to publish in the Gazette the name of each TP officer so empowered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: TP officers will continue to be empowered through appointment by the Deputy Commissioner of Police.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Clause 12 removes the provision that empowers TP to require vocational drivers to report to them and produce their fingerprints.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: This provision is obsolete, as TP already has the powers to compel any person, including vocational drivers, to report to TP and identify themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister of Home Affairs)
text: Clause 25 removes the provisions pertaining to the ticketing of traffic offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Over the years, TP has done exemplary work and, with its partners and the cooperation of the public, brought down road traffic fatalities significantly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the point that the hon Minister of State made just a few minutes ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is clear that there has been a downward trend over the past 10 years, even discounting last year where there was a circuit breaker imposed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, elderly pedestrians and motorcyclists continue to be involved in a disproportionate number of traffic accidents resulting in injuries or death.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is clear that legislation must not be the only policy instrument to protect our most vulnerable on the roads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Instead, there must be greater awareness, education and behavioural change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These informal norms work together with legislation to instil in each road user a culture of safety and mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is against this context that I now proceed to review the Bill, which I support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I start, however, by highlighting an area involving road safety that the Bill does not cover.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In August 2018, I spoke in Parliament about the need to hold vehicle owners and operators of vehicles involved in fatal accidents owing to mechanical failure liable – and criminally liable – for these accidents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This liability must be commensurate with the weight of consequences – I had highlighted specific cases where death was caused because of poorly maintained vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also articulated the need for legislation to cover the area.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Road Traffic Act focuses on driver conduct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Workplace Safety and Health Act focuses on vehicular accidents causing injuries to the employer's own workers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Neither applies to accidents that caused injury or death to third parties, owing to mechanical failure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We might argue, as the hon Senior Minister of State who replied to me then did, that we may rely on the Penal Code which makes it a crime for a person, who, through his rash or negligent act, causes death.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The same provisions may make corporations liable too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The problem, however, is that this is a general provision and a blunt instrument when it comes to a vehicle owner or operator in charge of maintenance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is needed is a specific provision that makes it clear that a vehicle owner is liable so long as the lack of maintenance played a contributory factor, it is not necessary that it plays an effective factor, which is the Penal Code's requirement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What I am arguing for, therefore, is a lower threshold on which liability can be proven.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also pointed out that it would be easy for a corporation to escape liability because of the absence of a provision in law to impute liability to corporations as a result of a default on the part of its employees for not maintaining the vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just earlier this year, I asked the hon Minister for Transport what is the average number of vehicles that caught fire per year in the last five years owing to mechanical failure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding that, I think it is safe to assume that a significant percentage of these fires are caused by poorly maintained vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) thinks so as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Its officers carry the buck of extinguishing such fires on roads and putting their own lives at risk and I think we should listen to them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In its own advisories, it states as follows: (a) most vehicle fires in Singapore occurred while the vehicles are travelling on the road; (b) the primary cause of these fires is due to ignition sources, such as overheating and electrical faults within the engine compartment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: SCDF also highlighted the need to service the vehicles regularly at authorised vehicle workshops to prevent vehicles from catching fire.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is time to make vehicle owners criminally responsible for fatalities and injuries arising from accidents caused by their poorly maintained vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also time for vehicle owners and workshop owners to be criminally liable if they have made illegal modifications to vehicles that are involved in accidents causing fatalities and injuries where these modifications played a contributing factor to the accidents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe this is the point that hon Member Mr Derrick Goh would expand on in his own speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With that, let me come to the Bill proper.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, on the point about ensuring pillion riders wear safety helmets, I obviously support that.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The issue I seek clarification on is the age of pillion riders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under paragraph 36 of Road Traffic Rules, it is stipulated that no person riding a motorcycle or scooter on a road shall carry any child below 10 years of age.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This affects the viability of parents escorting their children with PABs, especially school children in Primary schools.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would have thought that, if anything, it would be the other way around because the motorcyclist is likely to be travelling faster than a PAB rider.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, vehicle forfeiture in situations where the motorists engage in speed trials.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the stiffening of penalties for illegal speed trials.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They put other motorists and road users to great danger.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How about a situation where the owner did not know that his vehicle was being used by the offender but he was wilfully blind?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, he suspected, he could have asked but he did not.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, he did not specifically know that his vehicle was used by the offender.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for a clarification on the policy reason for the proposed change, as I understand the original reason for imposing mandatory forfeiture is to deprive would-be offenders from easily accessing vehicles for commission of offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third and finally, I come to the definition of a "responsible officer" under the proposed section 81 of the Road Traffic Act that the hon Minister of State outlined.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the proposed amendments, it is also provided that the owner should designate at least one of the responsible officers to ensure that a proper record is kept – it is a personal responsibility.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the hon Minister of State mentioned, failure to do so attracts liability, criminal liability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it not be sufficient to require that the board appoint an employee to be a responsible person?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is it possible to write in a provision to state that the responsibilities on these senior officers are discharged, once such an appointment is made?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Safety, respect for all users and a thoughtful, fair approach must govern the use of our roads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill gives us the promise of a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It solves some legal issues, but the need for public education, improving the safety culture and deepening the respect amongst road users – all those remain work-in-progress.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These tragic accidents could have been easily avoided.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I thus agree with the overall rationale underlying this Bill to enhance safety on our roads, as well as to strengthen security on our public transport.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I have some queries and concerns about the provisions relating to illegal car racing, giving of false information to Police and the expanded powers of search on bus and train commuters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister of State for Home Affairs highlighted that there has been an increased incidence of such offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In recent months, the public focus has been on the fatal crash at Tanjong Pagar that claimed five young lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Based on questions from other Members of this House, illegal car races may be taking place in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, I have also received significant feedback from residents about vehicles racing at high speeds within Aljunied GRC – such as along Tampines Road, the Upper Serangoon Road Viaduct and Lorong Ah Soo – several times a week.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While such an enhanced punishment will send a stronger deterrent signal to would-be offenders, I believe that those seeking such thrills will still try their luck, unless there is greater certainty of being caught.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister of State mentioned that there are currently about 300 cameras nationwide to detect such offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, could the Ministry confirm if law enforcement is stepping up further its capacity and operations to increase the likelihood of detecting illegal racing on our roads?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 20 of the Bill proposes to change the law regarding the offence of giving false information to Police about the identity of the driver who committed an offence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are aware of such cases where a vehicle owner falsely tells Police that another person was driving the vehicle in order that the owner escape punishment for a traffic offence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I agree with the proposed section 81(3A) which will make it an explicit offence for that other person to pretend or falsely represent that he was the driver.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He, too, will be liable for possible imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Hopefully, this will make it more difficult for vehicle owners to find fall guys to take the rap and thereby pervert the course of justice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note that just four years ago, the maximum fine had been raised from $1,000 to $5,000, a five-fold increase.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry clarify why there is a need to do so?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And, in particular, is there any indication that drivers are not deterred by the current levels of fines?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clauses 24 and 31 of the Bill provide for security screening of passengers upon entry into buses, bus interchanges, and trains and premises of the MRT and LRT.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although powers of search already exist in the Road Traffic Act and Rapid Transit Systems Act, these powers covered only passengers’ belongings but not searches of the passengers themselves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill will expand these powers to cover frisk searches of passengers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given the evolving security situation, including the threat from self-radicalisation, I do appreciate the rationale for this expanded power.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, I have a particular concern about these provisions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The term “frisk search” is defined in the Bill as “a search of an individual by quickly running the hands over the individual’s outer clothing”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Frisk searches thus involve physical contact with the person being searched.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My main concern revolves around the persons empowered to conduct frisk searches.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To explain the basis of my concern, allow me to briefly describe the various actors in our security landscape.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In our security eco-system, we have SPF officers, Auxiliary Police, unarmed security and other lay enforcement personnel.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The levels of training of these groups are vastly different.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Compulsory training of SPF officers requires six to nine months of residential training, while Auxiliary Police do residential training of eight to nine weeks or less than three months.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Unarmed security training can be completed in about a week or two.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I assume outsourced enforcement officers also undergo less intensive training.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Those with less training typically handle more routine tasks, such as controlling entry to premises, guarding installations or manning security equipment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, the SPF officers are expected to handle trickier situations involving the exercise of judgement and discretion and working with the community.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, over the years, there has been some convergence and overlap, as the training of APOs and unarmed security has been enhanced to enable them to perform more tasks than before.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the need to draw a line is still solid and sound.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is not clear to me that there is any requirement of seniority in the categories mentioned, so the term “senior approved persons” may, in fact, be a misnomer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, is enabling non-SPF actors to conduct frisk searches by force appropriate?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For comparison, let us look at another piece of legislation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This sensible demarcation is a recognition that a bodily search is an intimate security check which should only be performed by highly-trained persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill today marks a departure from that approach.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are Auxiliary Police, security officers and the outsourced enforcement officers suitable to perform frisk searches?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Do they have the requisite training, not only on how to perform the physical act of search, but also how to handle any confrontations that may arise?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another concern would be about searches on female commuters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Where are the precautions on how searches on women should be conducted, in order to have strict regard to decency?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since commuters have to comply, it is only reasonable that officers be easily identifiable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my opinion, requiring plainclothes officers to merely declare their office is not sufficient, and cases of impersonation of Police officers happen all the time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned about what these mean for safeguards for the commuter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, it is important that the provisions are coupled with strong capacities to detect offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is also critical to ensure that the risk of misuse of search powers on commuters is minimised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about the language for the theory tests for riders of Personal Mobility Devices (PMDs) and Power-assisted Bicycles (PABs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I commend the Ministry’s amendment to improve road safety by ensuring that PMD and PAB riders are well-equipped with a basic knowledge of the roads, just as all other vehicle riders already are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the cost of theory tests for PMD and PAB riders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we can see on the roads, a sizeable number of our PMB and PAB riders are food delivery riders who work tirelessly to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The test fees may be an additional cost and source of stress for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on the authorities’ power to conduct security checks on public transport.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 127B provides a uniformed officer and authorised employees the power to conduct frisk searches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such authorised employees, such as the bus operator, bus interchange operator, a security officer or an outsourced enforcement officer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 83 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) provides that women who are searched by a Police officer or ICA officer must be searched by a female officer, unless certain exceptions apply.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While maintaining the security of our public transport systems is vital, I believe it is equally important to maintain a sense of dignity for all women undergoing searches, which the new section 83 of the CPC addresses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify if a similar limitation applies to frisk searches under this Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, can the Ministry also commit to ensuring all relevant persons who may be considered an “approved person” under this amendment undergo the necessary training so that we can prevent instances where frisk searches are conducted erroneously?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is important for the safety of other road users as well as law and order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: After all, for our roads to be safe, the predictability of the behaviour of all road users must be there, at least to a large extent, barring a small number of errant users which should then be subject to the penalties of our laws.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The behaviour of many PAB users and, indeed, cyclists on the road seemed to imply that many riders either do not know the law or choose to disregard the law, for example, riders beating red lights or riding against traffic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At first glance, this may not be a bad idea though it will not be popular with some riders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would urge the Panel and the Government, in considering whether to have such requirements for cyclists or bicycles, to consider the regularity of breaches of Road Traffic and Active Mobility Rules by cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Ask ourselves whether we see such acts on an almost everyday or regular basis: beating red lights, cycling against traffic, cycling without helmets when on roads, not keeping on the left lane.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And how many of us cyclists actually know that it is, for example, illegal to cycle on the right side of a motor vehicle when not overtaking or planning to make a turn to the right?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We see frequent social media postings on some of these acts and even a small number of cyclists challenging riders or pedestrians when they were reminded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When there is consistent taking of liberties by cyclists, this factor should be taken into consideration for it reflects prevailing riding culture, the lack of respect for the law and consideration for other road or footpath users, not to mention the occasional road rage, in turn, tarnishes what many other road users think generally of cyclists and will breed a lack of respect for cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It does not help us cyclists in getting more respect and space from motorists on the road and even from pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I said that despite riding in East Coast Park since I was young, I had in later years avoided cycling there because it has become unsafe.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I said that cyclists do not always obey the directional signs or keep a proper lookout for pedestrians or other cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many pedestrians walk on or across the cycling path without caring for the safety of cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And I said that I have seen accidents in the park over the years, accidents that can be avoided if we had the right cycling culture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And I also said that the cycling culture in East Coast Park reflects the cycling culture nationally.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I said in my speech then that we missed a great opportunity to solve the problem back then in the mid-2000s.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In those days, the only people who seemed to have broken the law were elderly cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But after that, there was a huge influx of foreign workers and this meant a huge increase in the number of people using bicycles and many also followed the cycling culture, ignored the road safety rules because of lax enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And then from the late-2000s, with the increase in white collar foreign labour, we also saw many taking recreational road cycling at the same time as many Singaporeans did.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This was before e-bikes and e-scooters became popular.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, do we now think that we need to improve our riding culture or do we think it is merely only a small number of cyclists who flout the law and that we do not need to improve our riding culture?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The number of recreational cyclists and e-bikes has continued to increase.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government is building the much talked about extended cycling network.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In recent times, the Government has also talked about looking at having more dedicated cycling lanes, which are non-shared footpaths, and are looking at cycling lanes on selected roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But having more cycling lanes will not remove any existing cultural baggage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Riders, when left alone in such lanes, still need to be considerate, keep left, use the correct lights at night – which, by the way, many cyclists are not doing and there is inadequate enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many people are still not happy with sharing the use of footpaths with cyclists; and in my view, this stems from the issues of riding culture too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In recent years, the Government has had to deal with usage problems with our e-bikes and e-scooters, primarily stemming from a poor riding culture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It has been told to me in Parliament previously that the extended cycling network will not connect to the HDB blocks directly and there will still be a connection via footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, how do we ensure that PMD and PAB users will always dismount consistently and take a walk through the HDB block they are heading towards?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is part of the problem leading to their ban from footpaths eventually.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This, I think, is probably the most important and, arguably, the hardest objective we need to achieve.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have cited my speech from more than four years ago just to highlight for today's debate that the issue with riding culture has been a tenuous one for a long time due to years of inadequate action in the past.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Perhaps in the last four years, the Government has been too busy dealing with e-scooters after the Active Mobility Bill was passed, but I hope that the Government will address the riding culture once and for all for all groups.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is the thrust of the written Parliamentary Question I have filed for today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If people are used to riding in a certain way for years and they do not bother to find out about LTA's safe riding courses or go to the LTA's Facebook to watch their videos on these topics, how do you get the message to these people?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How do you tell them to stop beating red lights and cycling against the traffic, and to get a helmet or use bicycle lights?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On footpaths, how do you persuade the many pedestrians to keep left and for all users to be considerate to each other?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As a former Police officer and current unionist looking after the welfare of our transport workers, road safety is a topic very close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With close to a million road users plying our roads each day, we need to ensure that all of us get to our destinations safely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech today will focus on three key aspects where road safety can and must be improved – the safety of autonomous technologies, the safety of cyclists and power-assisted bicycle (PAB) users and the safety of our migrant workers when travelling to work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is to facilitate the conduct of AV trials in Singapore and to support research and development in the industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How are we doing in respect to other key countries racing to develop AVs, which will include the United States, Germany and the Netherlands?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Have our plans to trial autonomous public buses in Punggol, Tengah and the Jurong Innovation District been disrupted by the on-going COVID-19 pandemic?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If so, can LTA provide the new timeline for these trials to take place?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we continue to keep a keen eye on the development of AVs, it is also important that we look at the regulation of the Advanced Driver Assistance System, or ADAS.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I was deeply concerned to hear about a fatal car accident in the US in April, which involved a Tesla vehicle which was believed to be operating on autonomous mode.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While we impose strict safety standards on AV developers, how are we regulating seemingly conventional cars that are increasingly being equipped with new technologies, such as ADAS?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Car manufacturers have marketed such systems as an autopilot feature, which may give some drivers the illusion that they do not need to pay attention to the road when this feature is switched on.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that LTA could look seriously into this and review if there is a need for more regulation of such autopilot features and systems in cars.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The article speculated that the increase could be due to more people taking up cycling as a hobby due to the pandemic and being unfamiliar with safe riding habits on the road.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, to allow our public buses to have a safe and smooth journey during peak hours, the Road Traffic Act prohibits almost all vehicle types from plying the bus lanes during operational hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Cyclists, however, are allowed to cycle in the bus lanes in a single file.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The minimum width of our traffic lane is three metres and the average width of our public buses is around 2.5 metres.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is simply impossible for our buses to overtake cyclists safely without infringing into the next lane.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During bus lane operational hours, where there is peak hour traffic and where more buses are deployed, overtaking is both difficult and dangerous.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Cyclists, in particular amateurs, are especially vulnerable if they do not know how to navigate safely the blind spots of a big bus.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As Executive Secretary of the National Transport Workers' Union, my bus captains have told me repeatedly that they are seeing more cyclists on the bus lanes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many do not keep to the curb side and some ride two, or even three, abreast.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Bus captains worry for the safety of cyclists and other road users when attempting to overtake them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is both for their safety and also the safety of other road users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Less than a week later, there was another lorry accident which resulted in 10 migrant workers conveyed to the hospital.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The NTUC's Migrant Workers' Centre is assisting the injured workers in their recovery process and raising funds to help the families of the workers whose lives were lost in the tragic accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Safety concerns about how our workers are transported are not new.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Regulations were amended back in 2011, following a spate of fatal road traffic accidents involving workers then.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, the recent accidents are a grim reminder that trucks and lorries should only be used to transport goods and not people.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC is also engaging the relevant Government agencies to address implementation issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We want our workers to get to their workplaces and back home safely every day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While tripartite negotiations are underway, we should explore interim safety measures that can be adopted immediately.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, we call on employers to hire a dedicated driver to transport their workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is to eliminate the issue of driver fatigue.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many companies, especially those outside of the construction sector, still require their workers to double-hat as a driver after a tiring full work shift.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Drivers should also be required to have a vocational driving licence before they can transport passengers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a step-up from the current requirements for migrant worker drivers to pass the local Class 3 driving exam, as vocational training will focus on safety when transporting passengers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mandatory licensing also allows our authorities to screen and track drivers for any adverse driving records.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Co-mingling of goods and passengers is unsafe and is potentially fatal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If not properly secured, passengers risk being pinned by these heavy goods and machineries in the event of an accident, or even a sudden braking of the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Between goods and passengers, there should only be one onboard the vehicle at any one time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If employers persist to use lorries to transport their workers, we want to reduce the associated risks significantly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We can do so by securing the passengers with proper seat belts and by restricting the lorry's travelling speed when transporting workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In her earlier reply to Parliamentary Questions filed on this topic, Senior Minister of State Amy Khor highlighted that a workgroup had studied such issues back in 2008 and found that the cargo beds of lorries were not constructed in a manner for seat belts to be retrofitted safely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: That has been more than 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am glad that Senior Minister of State has indicated that the Ministry would review the issue again together with the tripartite partners and factor in new advancement in vehicle manufacturing and seat belt technology.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We also need to review the speed limit when passengers are on board goods vehicles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As Senior Minister of State Amy Khor mentioned, lorries are already subjected to a speed limit of 60 kilometres per hour.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Therefore, I do urge LTA to re-look the issue and limit the permissible travelling speed of lorries when they are used to transport passengers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I believe that this is a necessary price to pay to ensure the safety of the many workers who have left the comfort of their home country to help build our nation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Cyclists and PAB riders should not cycle on busy bus lanes during peak hours, and our migrant workers, and all workers, should have safer transport to work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, I want to thank Mr Dennis Tan for highlighting the importance of having a good riding culture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He also mentioned that he feels that licensing of bicycles and cyclists alone is not going to be effective because this needs to be accompanied by a safe riding culture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Dennis Tan also said that there needs to be enforcement going together with education.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Again, this is a point which I agree with him.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I just wanted to highlight, Mr Speaker, that I am not sure whether Mr Dennis Tan was in the Chamber earlier when I answered the Parliamentary Questions from Ms Poh Li San and Mr Gan Thiam Poh.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They filed questions on road cycling and on safety, and I answered their Parliamentary Questions earlier today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In my reply, I actually addressed some of these points that Mr Dennis Tan raised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I said, for example, that enforcement and education need to go hand in hand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I also talked about the practices in other countries, of how they promote cycling safety without having to license cyclists or bicycles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Importantly, I also acknowledged Mr Dennis Tan's written Parliamentary Question and I said – and if I may just read from my earlier reply: "In his written Parliamentary Question, Mr Dennis Tan asked if we have a public education campaign on safe practices for cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We formed the Active Mobility Advisory Panel in July 2015, more than five years ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The panel was set up precisely to bring together different groups of stakeholders to look at how to improve road safety and how to promote a safe riding culture, a point which I think Mr Tan also feels strongly about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the years, I think the Members of Parliament in this House from both the PAP and the Opposition – and I believe also our Nominated Members of Parliament – have raised concerns and given suggestions on how to improve road safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think this is something we should acknowledge and not give the wrong impression that suggestions, comments and proposals for enhancing safety have only come from the Workers' Party.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am excited and welcome the extension of the regulatory sandbox for a further five years.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: More synergistic cross-collaborations between the Traffic Police, LTA and AV developers would pave the way for better AVs that are road-safe-by-design.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This will inevitably lead to more instances of accidents involving cyclists and motorists.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It also means that when accidents happen involving a car and a cyclist, the cyclist will usually be at a greater risk.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In March 2021, a 42-year-old food delivery rider on an e-bike was killed following an accident with a Mini Cooper along Hougang Avenue.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: On 3 May 2021, a 49-year-old leisure cyclist was killed in an accident involving a shuttle bus at NTU.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: By all public accounts, she was a new cyclist who had only just bought her bicycle the week prior to the accident.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, the recommendation to have certifications for PAB users on roads is an important step towards improving the safety of motorists and cyclists on the road and is long overdue.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to these theory tests, may I also ask if there will be concomitant increased enforcement action and penalties on the road for errant cyclists as well?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I feel that this step has to go hand in hand with the education of cyclists to ensure that knowledge of good rider habits is put into practice.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Could I also ask if there may be provisions to improve accessibility for seniors to take this certification test?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the certifications could be conducted in various languages.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For the less digitally savvy seniors, could provisions also be given to allow them to take physical tests instead?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The costs of the certification renewal could also be kept low for the seniors or less abled who require use of the PABs for mobility.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The cost should also not be a hindrance to maybe food delivery riders who may need to depend on PABs for their livelihood.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, developments in the region have also required us to be more vigilant of possible threats from within or outside of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It has been deemed that there is a need to legalise security searches on a person on the public transport system.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The powers accorded to the officers seem wide-ranging.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, officers authorised to do such work must be well-trained in identifying suspects using objective criteria that must be set out beforehand.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially pertinent for the purposes of the revised section 127B, which empowers officers to frisk individuals and to request that one or more garments of the bus passenger or entrant – that may be conveniently removed – be removed and for the garment to be inspected.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In a multi-racial and multi-cultural society, we must always be mindful of actions that may imply racial or ethnic bias and constantly guard against it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it cannot be understated that clearly written policies on these details may be more important than ever.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There must also be set protocol and adequate infrastructure for the searches carried out by officers to be done in a dignified and respectful manner.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if searches have to be conducted on female commuters, should there also be some sort of initiative where when frisk searches are done, there should be some sort of recording which can protect the rights of the officers and commuters if there are any contentious reports?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Only when this is done will citizens be confident that decisions are made fairly and ensure public safety.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, in relation to safety on the roads, I would like to talk about the recent accidents that involved migrant workers on the roads.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Both left behind young families they were supporting.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, more than 20 others were injured in these accidents.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Just a few days ago, there was another accident involving a Police van and lorry, which left 17 men injured.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It seems like the measures we have in place may not be enough to protect the lives of these young men and this needs to change.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am cognisant that changes may incur more financial costs to the construction industry.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: But how do you determine the value of human lives?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I feel that any change in safety standards has to be legislated for it to be duly enforced.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: How can we make it safer for them?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The gold standard would be to use buses to transport them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware this means additional costs which are likely to be borne by all stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: With the rising property prices and delays in BTO flat completions, there will definitely be a further strain on everyone involved.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I believe that, as a modern, developed country, this is something we do have to work towards in the long term.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: But what can we do in the meantime?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I feel that this strengthens the finding that lorries are not safe for carrying people.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I echo what Member of Parliament Mr Melvin Yong has said previously – that trucks and lorries should only be used to transport goods and not humans.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There is a saying that safety rules are written in blood.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The rationale for introducing such a test of competence is to improve road safety and to make our roads and footpaths safer for pedestrians, riders and motorists.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I agree that we must take action to reduce the number of accidents on our roads and public paths, and my Workers’ Party colleagues have spoken about this matter on previous occasions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, how would the certification process be rolled out and the requirements phased in to ensure that all riders who wish to continue riding their vehicles are not left in a position where they are unable to obtain their certification before the requirements kick in?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially important as many riders do rely on their vehicles for work and to move around.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, in relation to the requirements to obtain certification, the Minister of State mentioned that there will be some form of safety code knowledge to be tested as part of the certification process.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But how would the test be tailored to allow for the specifics of riders, as opposed to more conventional road users, particularly in view that some of these riders will be allowed on public paths and roads?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also, would there be a minimum age and how will minors be regulated?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, on licensing, I would like to raise some concerns about the requirement for certification in general.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All of us in this House have residents who rely on these test-needed-to-ride-on-road vehicles for their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some of these delivery drivers rely on such vehicles as their sole source of income and some are sole breadwinners for their families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many older Singaporeans, too, rely on these vehicles to get around and they may not be so conversant in English.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, I have come across such residents who have shared with me their struggles in passing certification requirements in fields as diverse as chefs in the F&B industry to forklift drivers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of them have been doing these jobs for decades and excel with carrying out these jobs on a practical level, but struggle to pass the paper examinations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The result is often an impact on their livelihoods as they are unable to be employed in the very jobs they have been carrying on for years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that we learn from the experiences of our fellow Singaporeans who were affected by previous certification requirements and ensure that the certification process is simple enough so that it remains accessible to all of our residents and that they do not end up being unnecessarily tripped up by red tape.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The overriding objective of certification should be to raise awareness of road safety and to educate, not to treat it like an examination to score road users.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Will there be the option to take the test in languages which our older Singaporeans are more conversant in?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What provisions will be made for the small minority of riders who may not be so literate and able to sit a test?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What assistance will they be given to learn and understand the safety requirements in order to be able to pass the test?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, I would like to move on to another large theme of the Bill before us: the theme of enhancing road safety.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There are many provisions being introduced through the Bill, from enhancing safety for our road users to ensuring the security or safety of persons who use our public transport networks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, there is one area of safety which does not feature and that is the safety of migrant workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These workers were riding in the backs of lorries, in an area meant for cargo.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This issue has been under scrutiny for over a decade, with calls stemming back to 2009 being made – many by colleagues in this House – to ban the transport of workers in the backs of lorries like livestock or goods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must not forget that these are workers who leave behind their homes and families and slog for long hours under all weather conditions to build our homes and to repair our roads.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such a practice is dangerous to not only the migrant workers themselves, but it also poses real risks to other road users.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As mentioned previously, this topic has been debated as far back as 2009, and yet 12 years, and numerous other deaths and injuries later, we are still arguing about whether this is an appropriate way to treat migrant workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I am glad to hear that NTUC is looking at this matter, I note that the reason always given whenever such calls are being made is that to allow any safer ways of transporting migrant workers would mean increased costs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Leaving aside what this says about us as a country where we can argue that "increased costs" is a good enough reason to turn a blind eye to lower safety standards for "lower tier workers", I believe this argument is flawed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, because it ignores a more fundamental problem in our labour system that we are still struggling to address and that is our addiction to cheap labour, often at the expense of productivity increases.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Despite many pointing out the danger and unsustainable nature of our approach of importing cheap labour in sectors, such as the construction and marine industries, not much has been done by enterprises to shift away from this model towards a more productive, less labour-intensive model.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While this is a topic for another day, it would naturally flow that any increased costs by more stringent transport safety standards would have less of an impact if we are not so reliant on employing a large force of cheap, low-skilled workers in our building sector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, as we have been looking at our ITM 2.0 roadmaps, is this not a good time for us to start looking into the entire way the construction industry is structured, to really find long-lasting, sustainable solutions that maximise productivity and minimise labour input?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, this argument is also problematic, as we did not shy away from mandating safety measures, such as seat belts on all school buses, when an accident, which killed an 8-year-old boy in 2008, saw a retrofitting of seat belts on all school buses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is actually a non-starter, as the statistics quoted include the number of injuries for all road users, and crucially include motorcycles, which have a higher casualty rate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, as the Senior Minister of State Amy Khor said yesterday, each life lost leaves behind a family that is grieving and each injury has the potential to leave a worker unable to continue working to support his family.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Referring to other countries where such similar practices are allowed should not be our first reaction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Why do we not instead compare ourselves to countries which better respect the safety of such workers by holding ourselves to the same high safety standards of those countries?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The drop in tourism due to COVID-19 has resulted in many buses and mini-buses with spare capacity – perhaps this is a good time as any to start the transition, with some kind of Government support.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The re-purposing of such currently idle or under-utilised buses or mini-buses would be welcomed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am glad to hear from Senior Minister of State Amy Khor that this will be one of the matters to be considered.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Last but not least, I turn to the extension of frisking powers to "authorised persons" mentioned in clauses 20, 24 and 31 of this Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Subsection 9 of the new section 23A of the Bill defines these "authorised persons" as: one, an officer or an employee of the Authority; two, an employee of an auxiliary police force in uniform; three, an employee of a licensee authorised to operate a rapid transit system using train or railway premises; four, a security officer (within the meaning of the Private Security Industry Act) engaged by a licensee mentioned in paragraph (c); and five, an outsourced enforcement officer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While there are good reasons to step up security due to persistent concerns about terrorism and the security of our transport networks, this amendment continues the trend of expanding key Police powers to persons who may not be fully trained in law enforcement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As in previous cases of extending Police powers, the language of the Bill does not discuss the training that these “authorised persons” will receive to exercise their powers with sufficient care and due diligence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Police powers must be wielded judiciously and carefully, and adequate training must be given to counter the risk of abuse, including but not limited to excessive enforcement, harassment and even sexual assault, particularly in view of the inclusion of frisk searches; this is very important.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Because of these concerns, could we not directly build safeguards into the relevant provisions?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another example would be to use body cams to reduce the likelihood of abuse and overly vigorous use of such powers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some further concerns that I have include confusion or lack of awareness by members of the public should they be stopped and searched.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This may lead to such incidents accumulating and, ultimately, will prove damaging to social cohesion in Singapore, while undermining trust in actual law enforcement officers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In July 2010, a Parliamentary Question was asked of the Minister for Transport to consider legislating that employers must transport their workers in buses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite these vehicle-related safety measures, driver-related measures, enforcement and penalties and public education, we are continuing to see fatalities and injuries from workers being transported on lorries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workplace Safety and Health Act imposes a duty on employers to take reasonably practicable measures to ensure the safety and health of persons at work.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers facing environments, such as working at heights, lifting operations and operating heavy machinery, must put in place safety measures, and these have prevented needless injuries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: WSH 2028 vision works towards reducing Singapore’s workplace fatality rate to less than one per 100,000 workers by 2028, and a pervasive adoption of the Vision Zero culture where stakeholders are committed to preventing all forms of injury and ill-health at work.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is clear that the current measures for transporting workers as passengers on goods vehicles is not enough and must be improved.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has taken strong action in the past in reaction to deaths that could have been prevented.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After a fatal school bus accident in 2008, seat belts for small school buses were made compulsory in 2009.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
