text: We should now similarly prioritise human lives over increased costs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Financial assistance for businesses with difficulties complying can be explored.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can also explore whether there is spare capacity in the form of tour buses now under-utilised that will make this a good time to implement new measures.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The workers affected are primarily migrant workers, who form one of the most vulnerable groups in our society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The neglect of their protection and welfare has long been a bone of contention in our society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Reactive responses only when death occurs in traffic accidents, domestic helper abuse or dormitory infections are not enough.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can MOT let us know how much time is needed for this review?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lives are at stake here and we hope for speedy action to be taken.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further to the issue of safe transportation of workers, Progress Singapore Party would like to highlight that this would be a good time for a holistic review of all the areas related to the protection of migrant workers, for example, dormitory conditions, recruitment costs, job mobility and strengthening enforcement of breaches by employers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, as a union leader, I am aware that this amendment would affect the freelance and self-employed delivery riders who ride road-only power-assisted bicycles, or PABs for short.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Just less than one and a half years ago, many of these vocational riders transited from Personal Mobility Devices to PABs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: They are, therefore, concerned with the increasing regulations and its impact on their source of income and livelihood.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure that vocational PAB riders are adequately prepared to meet this new requirement, I would like to call for Government assistance to equip them with the appropriate learning tools and relevant training to cater to the needs of the vocational riders.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The current Safe Riding Programme offered by LTA is more suited for the general population.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC will work closely with MOT and LTA to better support them through the training programme and eventually passing the competency test.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC is also working with LTA to ensure that while the questions in the competency test address the appropriate standards of road and public path safety, the questions will also be manageable for PAB riders to comprehend and answer.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With the passing of the Bill, adequate support should be provided for the riders and the new regulations should not impede the workers' source of income and their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to touch on another aspect that is close to my heart and the heart of the workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As we push to enhance the safety of our road users and pedestrians, let us also pay attention to the safety of our freelance and self-employed workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Amongst the vocational PAB riders, food delivery riders are heavy and frequent road users with long hours of riding and have a higher risk of getting into an accident.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure that their families worry for them every day.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike a regular or contract employees, freelance and self-employed workers do not enjoy the statutory benefits provided for under the Work Injury and Compensation Act, or WICA, for work-related injuries.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: More needs to be done to ensure freelance and self-employed workers are compensated for work-related injuries.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):    Let me now say a few words in Malay.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As I have shared in my English speech, I acknowledge that the Road Traffic (Amendment) Bill would affect the freelance and self-employed delivery riders who ride road-only power-assisted bicycles.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure that vocational riders are adequately prepared to meet this new requirement, I would like to call for Government assistance to equip them with the appropriate learning tools and relevant training.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC will be working closely with the relevant agencies to better prepare the affected workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As we push to enhance the safety of our road users and pedestrians, let us also pay attention to the safety of our freelance and self-employed workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, these workers are not compensated for work-related injuries – more needs to be done to protect them.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, with this, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC looks forward to working closely with the relevant agencies to better prepare the affected workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, as more cyclists take to the roads, there has been an increase in hostility between cyclists and motorists, and even pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments are aimed at making the roads and pavements safer for everyone.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The conduct of cyclists on the roads has been the topic of frequent, sometimes intense, debates on social media.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the course of policymaking, we need to take into consideration the views of cyclists as well as other road users.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, we want safety for all road users.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Since we have identified cycling as an important element in our move towards a car-lite nation, we cannot and should not relegate cyclists to the pavements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their behaviour, decisions and actions can give rise to accidents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have four recommendations to promote safe and responsible cycling.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must work on creating more dedicated cycling lanes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many cities around the world, including Singapore, are experiencing a cycling boom since the COVID-19 pandemic started.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is largely driven by anxiety over shared enclosed spaces on board public transportation and a heightened interest in outdoor exercise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am glad to hear last week that LTA is considering converting sections of roads as well as the removal of roadside parking spaces, to make way for cycling tracks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The city saw a massive commuter shift to bicycles during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Paris is a bustling metropolis with existing buildings and infrastructure in place – very much like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: New cycling infrastructure will take years, even decades, to complete if they are to be built from scratch.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I, therefore, urge our Government to consider this initiative seriously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would be helpful if the cycling community can be involved and assist the LTA in identifying routes where dedicated cycling lanes can be created.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From LTA enforcement reports, I understand that it is an offence to cycle against traffic flow.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, this is not immediately obvious to all cyclists.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is no explicit statement about riding against traffic flow in Section III of the Highway Code, which is widely assumed to be the only piece of law that governs conduct on the roads, nor is there anything on LTA's website about cycling on roads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Unless someone is a lawyer or works at LTA, one might not be aware that there may be multiple sources of the law relating to cycling.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some cyclists, therefore, may break the rules because they are genuinely uninformed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Others may exploit the lack of clear information and do as they please.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This creates confusion and dangerous situations on the roads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A suggestion would be to further enhance the Road Traffic Act, specifically, to ensure that the Act is explicitly clear that it covers cyclists the same way as it does for motorists.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Once that is achieved, we can then work on raising awareness that the law applies equally to cyclists as well.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, motorists should be educated on the hand signals that cyclists use so that the intentions of cyclists are clear to motorists.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note with concern that there is a divergence between recommendations within the cycling community and the guidelines for cyclists on LTA's website.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, LTA's website states that cycling two abreast is allowed on non-single lane roads and on bus lanes outside their operational hours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, many people, including cyclists, believe that cycling should always be done in a single file.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In fact, the Highway Code requires cyclists to "ride in a single file when possible".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Divergence results in one side assuming that the other is not compliant, thereby resulting in conflicts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should align guidelines and recommendations for cyclists on the roads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should avoid referring to road traffic rules as guidelines or as a code.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to avoid any ambiguity as to their applicability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They should be clearly stated as laws to be adhered to and to be included in common road user education and theory tests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if these rules are broken, the offenders should be brought to task.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On one hand, in cycling-friendly cities like the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany, the concept of presumed liability is practised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This means that in an accident, the burden of proof is shifted from the more vulnerable road user like a pedestrian or cyclist to the driver of motor vehicles, such as cars and lorries, which are capable of causing more impact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This rule does not automatically abolish fault or impose liabilities over any single party.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The accused may still disprove claims of fault in Court.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Legislating for presumed liability may, indeed, help accelerate the progress of Singapore as a car-lite nation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the sheer amount of existing conflict between cyclists and motorists in Singapore, imposing a similar law may now widen the rift.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it is certainly something we should consider as part of improving safety and responsibility among users of shared roads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, the concept of duty of care in common law already requires a driver and, indeed, all road users, to adhere to a reasonable standard of care when using the roads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But ultimately, the "motorists versus cyclists" situation will never improve if we do not change our attitudes about each other to be more gracious and accommodating on the roads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The "me first" culture on our roads must stop.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Every single road user – motorists, cyclists or pedestrians – has a personal responsibility to reshape our road safety culture.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Be kind, be patient and be considerate to one another.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In doing so, we can improve road safety in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Given the number of accidents involving cyclists, this could help ensure that cyclists are well-acquainted with the relevant regulations, thereby improving road safety for all users.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: However, apart from licensing and certification, perhaps we could look into improving road infrastructure as another possible solution.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As the Government seeks to promote active mobility amongst the public, it is crucial to ensure that our infrastructure will be able to keep pace with the expected increase in individuals opting for such modes of transport.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As part of these efforts, could the Ministry also consider studying the possibility of repurposing car lanes into bike lanes?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This could potentially improve connectivity for cyclists while also contributing to road safety.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: While the Government embarks on projects to improve our infrastructure for cyclists, I hope that the Ministry can also factor in the needs of cyclists who are persons with disabilities to ensure that infrastructure in the pipeline is inclusive.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Thus, while their disabilities may be invisible to some, research has shown that people with disabilities have a disproportionately higher need for protected cycling infrastructure and direct routes.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Obstacles, uneven surfaces and gradients could potentially cause discomfort to disabled cyclists or inadvertently exclude them from using the cycling paths as they may not be able to lift or push their bicycles.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Infrastructure should also be designed to be able to accommodate wider, non-standard cycles, such as tricycles, tandems and recumbents.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: On the expansion of search and seizure powers, while I understand the need for such measures to strengthen the preparedness of our public transport system against security threats, I have several queries for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: My first query relates to the training which will be provided to "approved persons", especially for those who are not Police officers or employees of an Auxiliary Police Force.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Could the Minister share more about the training which approved persons will receive before they are authorised to frisk search commuters, if any?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: More specifically, does the Ministry intend to provide training and introduce guidelines to ensure the appropriateness and proportionality of action taken in relation to the assessed threat level?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This could help prevent cases of abuse of authority, which include excessive behaviour, harassment or even sexual assault.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, how would the Ministry minimise the profiling of minorities and marginalised persons which may inadvertently arise in the process of identifying commuters to undergo additional security screening?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Such profiling might amount to over-policing and could potentially be damaging to our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The second query I have relates to public awareness and education.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Given that security checks can be conducted by Police officers who are not in uniform, as well as approved persons authorised by LTA in writing, how would commuters be assured that officers who are conducting these security checks are legitimate?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: How would commuters know if officers are behaving in an appropriate manner?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Does the Ministry intend to provide avenues for commuters to seek recourse and remedies should they encounter inappropriate actions taken by these officers?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: On top of introducing safeguards to minimise the occurrence of such incidents, I hope that the Ministry will also consider conducting public education campaigns so that commuters can be aware of their rights with regard to security screening and frisk searches proposed by this Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: PABs are commonly used by delivery staff and it is not easy for them to make ends meet in this difficult economic climate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am thus very concerned about the affordability of the tests and would propose that it be set at an affordable level.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also urge companies who engage these essential workers to pay for the costs of the tests on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, there are dangers posed by helmets which do not meet regulatory requirements or are of unsuitable sizes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have seen children pillion riders wearing helmets which are too big for them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that motorcyclists provide their pillion riders with the correct type of helmets?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will there be more public education programmes to highlight the importance of wearing right-sized helmets?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am very concerned about the safety of young motorcycle pillion riders, some of whom are only in pre-school or Primary school.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider mandating the wearing of the correctly-sized helmets?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I support this measure to ward off potential security attacks, I have concerns about imposters taking advantage of passengers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the Bill had stated, these personnel may or may not be in uniform, so it is really not easy for commuters to tell if they are genuine.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Molesters or pickpockets may pretend to conduct frisk searches.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister share what measures are in place to reduce the likelihood of this happening?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I would like to touch on the proposed amendment regarding the forfeiture of vehicles used for illegal road races.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On one hand, this seems to be fair to the owners but, on the other hand, there may be instances where owners of the vehicles claim that they did not provide consent in order to keep the vehicles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, in reality, they had given consent and provided the offending driver access to the vehicle.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would the Ministry be able to separate the genuine cases from the non-genuine ones?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Many delivery staff for goods and meals use PABs to earn a living.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I urge the authorities to ensure that the test fees are affordable to them and I also urge companies which engage their services to pay the fees for them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am also worried about the safety of young pillion riders on motorcycles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of them are Primary school students who wear helmets which are too big.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider requiring them to wear right-sized helmets?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill will empower Police officers and authorised personnel to conduct security screening of bus and MRT commuters.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As for the clause concerning the forfeiture of vehicles involved in illegal racing, I would like to ask the Minister how the Ministry would distinguish whether the owner of the involved vehicle did or did not provide consent to the offending driver.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During the circuit breaker period, we have seen videos of an illegal street race along KPE where six men and two women were eventually arrested.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The roads of Lim Chu Kang, Seletar, Tuas have been observed at times to be used for drag competition, with multiple cars gathering at these locations to watch the race.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And how can we forget the shocking deaths of five young men earlier this year after they sped through Tanjong Pagar?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These illegal racers not only put themselves at serious risk of harm, but also expose other road users and innocent bystanders to these risks.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I understand that some people are passionate about cars, these racing-related activities do not have a place on our public roads.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have been lucky thus far that no innocent bystanders have been hurt, which makes it even more important for us to act now to ensure that our roads remain safe for everyone who use them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, to keep our roads safe, I am in support of the increased penalties for racing and speed trials.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, to ensure that the right punishment is meted out to the right individual, I am also in support of the stiffer penalties for individuals who mislead the Traffic Police in their investigations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, I am in support of disqualifying motorists for road rage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to seek some clarification on this matter.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What if the accused was a cyclist exhibiting road rage to a motorist?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure the consequence to cyclists and motorists can be equally meted out as we have seen videos of cyclists verbally abusing and punching motorists on several occasions already?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I support the penalisation of motorists who fail to ensure their pillion wears an approved helmet and the introduction of stiffer penalties for those selling poor quality non-approved helmets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I think that this legislation would provide a good baseline safety standard for helmets that should be used on our roads and improve the overall safety of our motorcyclists and their pillions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would also like to seek clarification on the penalising of motorcyclists who fail to ensure their pillion wears an approved helmet as well as the stiffer penalties for those selling non-approved helmets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I appreciate and understand the intent in ensuring that helmets pass certain safety standards so that they can protect both rider and pillion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Singapore, the standards follow the TUV SUD PSB Standard.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It involves one-drop test on the front, back and side of the helmet, a penetration test using a sharp object falling on the helmet and a chin strap test using a weight pulling on the strap.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These tests are conducted in batches, meaning dealers have to put about 1% to 4% of each batch of helmets that they bring in, that they import in, through these destructive tests.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is also an additional stamp duty of S$110.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The high price, compulsory batch destructive testing and the small market make helmet testing an economical burden to both the dealers and the riders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The dealers will have to then pass on this cost to the riders and this may be a deterrent to the riders, especially if we have riders from the lower income group.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, while we seek to ensure better safety standards for more of our motorcyclists and their pillions, the economics of testing may hinder the intent of the legislation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given Singapore's small motorbike market compared to the world, by requiring an additional destructive test on an already small batch of helmets increases the helmet price prohibitively and may act as a deterrent for motorcyclists to get the good helmets that can keep them safe.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One way we can overcome this is if we can consider accepting other standards that are internationally accepted.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Renowned bike helmet manufacturers like Shoei and Arai that are declared safe for MotoGP use, the "Formula 1" of motor racing, usually come with the ECE or SNELL standards.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: ECE refers to the Economic Commission for Europe safety standard, which is used by more than 50 countries, including Europe, and recognised by international racing bodies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: World safety standards for helmets also include the US Department of Transportation (DOT) and SNELL standards.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also consider motorcyclists who have already purchased such high-end helmets with internationally-accredited standards but without the soon-to-be mandatory PSB certification.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It would be economically costly for these motorcyclists to have to purchase yet another helmet when the present high-end helmet they have, such as those produced by Arai and Shoei, are already internationally-certified as safe.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If, however, the concern was counterfeit products from these renowned manufacturers, perhaps the Ministry can consider dealers showing proof of source direct from manufacturer.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The challenge of scale in Singapore's small domestic bike market is even more evident if special helmets are required.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, since the demand for a good kid's pillion helmet is small in Singapore, it does not make economic sense for a dealer to provide for PSB-approved kids' helmets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This may subsequently result in the child riding pillion having to wear an ill-fitting, oversized PSB-approved helmet as compared to a correct fitting helmet approved by the ECE or SNELL standards.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This seems counter intuitive to the intent of the legislation, which is to improve the safety of our motorcyclists and their pillions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a Facebook video created by content creator TRI333PLE for the motorcycling community, the video showed how some expensive high-end helmets with SNELL and ECE certification performed better at impact testing as compared to cheaper PSB-approved helmet.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As mentioned by a few riders, Mr Imran Ayub and Mr Sultan Shaheed, they want to be given the opportunity to provide the best safety gear for themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many welcome the new legislation for PABs as yet another way to keep our roads and pedestrian walkways safe.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We just have to consider the many Foodpanda and GrabFood drivers who use PABs to do their deliveries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For such cases, how soon can they sign up and go for the test such that their income will not be inadvertently affected by this new legislation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should they fail the first-time round, how soon can they book for a subsequent test?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are we able to conduct these PAB tests using vernacular languages for those who are not as comfortable with English as a medium of instruction?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another consideration is the cost element of such tests.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How affordable will it be for people who really depend on the PABs for their livelihood?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is there a chance that we can provide subsidies, possibly via SkillsFuture, to defray the costs of these tests?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we improve the safety of our roads and pedestrian walkways, let us not put such groups that depend on the PABs for their livelihood at a disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us try to make it as quick and convenient as possible for them to get their certification so that they can continue using their PABs safely for their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):    Illegal racers not only put themselves at a serious risk but also expose road users and those who are innocent to this risk.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To keep our roads safe, I support higher penalties for racing and speed tests.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With regard to the higher penalties for unapproved helmets, I would like to seek a clarification.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe this law will provide a good basic safety standard for helmets while improving the safety of motorcyclists and pillion riders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, there are also helmets that are safer and conform to international standards, such as ECE and SNELL.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: High-end helmets, such as Shoei and Arai, often come in limited numbers to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the fees and destructive testing required for PSB certification, it may not be economically practical to conduct destructive testing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The new laws for power-assisted bicycles, or PABs, are another way to keep our roads and pedestrian footpaths safe.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, many people, like Foodpanda and GrabFood deliverers, rely on PABs to earn a living.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can they register immediately and undergo tests as soon as possible so that their incomes will not be affected by this new law?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we conduct these PAB tests in the vernacular languages, such as Mandarin, Malay, Hokkien and so on, especially for those who are uncomfortable using the English language?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another consideration for the PAB test is its affordability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In our efforts to improve safety on the roads and pedestrian footpaths, let us ensure that these PAB tests are affordable and can be taken easily so that they can continue to use PABs for their jobs as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mr Speaker, Sir, the increased penalties for racing, time trials and road rage will assist to make our roads safer.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Over the years, this Government has put much effort into improving road safety through legislation as well as through non-legislative efforts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Based on Traffic Police statistics, the efforts have shown to be effective.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While traffic fatalities have steadily declined over the last 10 years in absolute terms and a similar downtrend is seen in road traffic injuries sustained, this improvement is even more significant if one considers the other side of the equation – that both road traffic and users have also increased.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the limited road capacity in Singapore and increased road traffic and shared usage, I am glad that we have continued to re-assess our approach in response to the evolving trends and threats in road safety.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments to the Road Safety Act, or RTA, tabled in this House today are even-handed in approach, with enhanced penalties for higher risk areas, recalibrating penalties, for example, in vehicle forfeiture to reduce prejudice faced by non-complicit vehicle owners and added new offences as well as requirements factoring new trends related to road traffic usage.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This legislation has also added new offences as well as requirements factoring the increase in PABs on the road.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I will now speak on the specific amendments.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On the issue of enhancing penalties for the existing offence of importing or selling unapproved helmets, I welcome this move.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This amendment is an enlightened approach by looking more strategically at the supply chain to signal to both importers as well as sellers that the sale of unapproved helmets will not be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Turning to the increase in penalties for illegal speed trials, I believe that this sends a strong signal to racers that their anti-social behaviour on the roads attract consequences.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Apart from the obvious endangerment to life, illegal speed trials create other social ills that affect even more people in Singapore and, that is, noise pollution.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Similar to Members of this House who have spoken on this topic before me, my residents at Nee Soon have shared that they are often woken up by the sounds of loud revving cars and motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is due to motorists speeding from Yishun Dam to Avenue 1 in Yishun outside their homes in the wee hours of the morning.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These modifications include illegally modified engines and exhaust systems which are the source of noise pollution, causing public nuisance as well as enhancing engine power settings that increase the safety risks to the driver and other road users.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In trying to stem illegal vehicle modification, it was discussed in this House last March and the RTA was updated in 2017 to give more teeth to enforcement efforts against errant workshops to deter them from offering such services.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While enforcement against errant workshops can be challenging, I applaud LTA for some success in stemming this activity at the source.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the above, could the Minister of State consider more effective measures to be put in place to address this through better detection instead of what seems to be mainly an enforcement approach which is a cat-and-mouse game that is resource-intensive?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If our traffic enforcement officers are able to identify illegal vehicle modifications at roadblocks in the early hours of the day, one would expect vehicle inspection centres with specialised equipment to better detect such modifications to engine as well as exhaust systems even if they are not easily visible.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, the vehicle noise test could perhaps be done under more realistic conditions where a vehicle is put under load and accelerated on a rolling stock to detect the “pop and crackle” sound.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope more thought can be given to how we may overcome these challenges through better detection and if the Minister can provide further updates on this to better protect road users as well as our community.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On the topic of introducing a single theory test for PABs on the roads, I believe this would be helpful in ensuring that PAB users are aware of the road traffic rules and behave in a safe manner on the roads.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, I note that the theory test is envisaged to be online and the results are valid lifelong.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I raise three questions for clarification on how this would be operationalised, as I am sure the public would be very interested.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One, if the test is to be done online, whether there will be special arrangements made for those who are not tech-savvy or not as literate, such as our elderly PAB users?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, whether the test will involve a fee and, if it does, are there ways to either subsidise or waive the fee so as not to impose a burden on residents, especially those in financial difficulties?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Before I end my speech, I wish to briefly mention about the issuance of fines for offences committed under the RTA.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel that this test will be very helpful.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As PABs can be used on both roads and shared paths, it is prudent and necessary to ensure that the riders are thoroughly educated on safety measures, potential risks, road etiquette and regulations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They will benefit from understanding the importance of compliance, which will enhance road safety for themselves and other road users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the theory test be conducted in languages other than English for non-English speaking applicants?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider making oral tests available as well?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, will the Government require riders who had been caught flouting traffic regulations to go for refresher training?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As many PABs are used by riders on delivery platforms, there is a need for these tech companies to review their reward systems, so that the riders will not be speeding to meet clients’ expectations at the expense of public safety and their own lives.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The delivery charges could be based on mileages between points at a reasonable and compliant speed limit.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Otherwise, tech companies could be equally liable for offences if their systems encourage excessive risk-taking at the expense of public safety.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the past year, PABs have increased in number – especially as many use it as a form of transportation on public roads.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was, no doubt, driven by the increase in the demand for food delivery services, which, in turn, led to a rise in the ownership and usage of PABs as food delivery riders saw PABs as providing a quick, convenient and fairly affordable method for them to fulfil their orders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With this increase in numbers of PAB riders over the years, I believe it is now useful for us to review the Road Traffic Act and introduce amendments to better safeguard the well-being of PAB riders and also other commuters and users of the road.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, as Minister of State Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim mentioned, PAB riders are required to pass a theory test before they can ride on cycling paths.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a much welcome move as casual observations would tell us that many PAB riders have been riding on the roads even before the introduction of such a mandatory qualifying test.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have seen, over the years, many fatal and near-fatal accidents involving PABs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Implementing a qualifying test that aims to inculcate road awareness, defensive riding and road use safety would certainly help to alleviate the situation if PAB riders are now going to be more aware about riding and road use etiquette.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, training PAB riders, Mr Speaker, is only one part of the solution.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more PAB riders on the road, other vehicular road users must also be more aware and mindful of their presence and learn to co-share the road with them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would there be plans to update the existing training curriculum of motorists to inculcate greater awareness in our present road users – our motorists – about the presence of this new group of road users, such as PAB riders, and even regular cyclists, who are also increasingly making their presence felt on the roads as well?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If there are plans to translate the handbook into other languages, when would these handbooks be made available, either online and possibly offline as well, in the form of a physical handbook?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, will the proposed tests be as challenging as the motorists' Highway Code test, which, although I have not taken for quite a few years now, I understand does require some time and effort to study and prepare for?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are cases of people who actually fail to pass the Highway Code test.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While these tests are currently going to be done online, would there be the option of written or even oral tests for those who might not be so comfortable with the digital testing option?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given that riders of these vehicles – motorcycles and scooters – need to pass practical tests before they are allowed on the road, does the Government foresee users of road-travelling PABs needing some sort of simplified or modified practical test or some basic practical training in terms of how they should manage their PAB on the road?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Riding on the road and riding on cycling paths are two very different experiences.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If one of the aims of this Bill is to ensure the safety of the PAB riders, then perhaps PAB riders should be educated on how to ride on the road before actually being allowed on the road.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps this education could take the form of some sort of practical experience, as onerous as that may sound.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the authorities intend to ensure that all riders are certified before they ride on the roads and how would this enforcement be done?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The implementation of self-driving technology will have a huge impact on our transport system.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: AVs will provide a much-needed solution to the shortage of manpower resources required in public transportation, goods delivery and industries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With recharged power, the AV fleet is able to operate 24/7 with no rest days required and no human resource headaches.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the long run, as AVs proliferate, we can expect to see lower costs of operations, higher productivity, enhanced convenience in last-mile connectivity and better control of road safety.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The benefits of AVs are clear and the vision of future roadways operated by a mixed-use traffic is compelling.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, the journey is still fraught with many uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, the roadmap to achieve a stable AV system remains unknown.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Back in the early 2000s, even though Singapore does not have a vehicle manufacturing industry, we chose the uphill path to be an innovation leader instead of being a technology adopter.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Recently, Hyundai announced that they will build an innovation centre in Singapore to manufacture electric vehicles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must take advantage of our well-developed transport system and implement AVs as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We do have a conducive innovation eco-system, including a sandbox to trial AV operations and push technological boundaries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In transportation, safety is key and vehicle reliability is critical.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Roadways are a complex intersection of motorists, cyclists, commuters and pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Even though there is only one set of traffic rules, the human response can be varied and not everyone will always follow the rules.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: That is why it is so challenging to integrate machine-coded logic in AVs into the dynamic roadway system.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Any mishap or a possible accident can easily derail many years of efforts to build safety, reliability and trust in AVs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Till date, a safety driver behind the wheel is still necessary.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is because equipment and systems can sometimes fail too.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must adapt AVs to our road users and continue to train more bus drivers to be AV bus safety operators.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The designated trial zone we have will allow a gradual phasing in of AVs and for the engineers to understand how AVs can be improved.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This extension will allow time for our AV engineers and land transport regulators to better understand and ensure smooth and safe operations before providing any approvals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In fact, I would suggest for LTA to consider extending the sandbox to other parts of Singapore where the roadway conditions may differ slightly from different parts of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The sandbox extension will also give space and time for road users to gain confidence and for AVs to make that ultimate big leap towards the day when safety drivers are no longer required.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the next five years, engineers and regulators will validate how the AV technology can be applied safely towards our robust mixed-use traffic operations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: A traffic accident involving an AV and a car driven by a human is not as straightforward as two human drivers involved in an accident.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For instance, if there should be a malfunction of the AV leading to an accident involving deaths, would the owner or the manufacturer of the AV be liable?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This aspect is as complex when compared to technology and safety development.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The legal liability and insurance framework cannot be considered without the full understanding of the design and AV technology.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I would hope MOT and the relevant Ministries are able to provide us with some information about AV legal protection and insurance coverage.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Every gamechanger will have its boons and its banes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Just like the adoption of digital technology, the disruptive nature of AVs will have some drivers losing their jobs once the technology is implemented on our roads.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some residents in Sembawang West have shared with me their concerns regarding their livelihoods once AVs are implemented on our roads.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As we extend the duration of the sandbox, let us all think out of the box to carefully plan ahead to be ready for a new equilibrium on our roads.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Human drivers and driving machines will co-exist and this sandbox must not become a Pandora's Box.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will also speak on how we can and need to go beyond the current set of amendments to improve the safety and working conditions of these delivery riders using PABs as a working tool.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My fellow Labour Members of Parliament and I have spoken in Parliament on various occasions for the protection of platform workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These workers make up a sizeable proportion of Singapore's growing gig economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is necessary to build a better eco-system of support for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Clearly, more competent delivery riders translate into enhanced safety for all road users, including drivers and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The online theory test also underscores the duty of PAB riders to be more responsible to other road users.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our aim is not to unduly penalise delivery riders, but to ensure that they are well-equipped with the requisite knowledge to enhance their safety on the road.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the theory test can be taken from 30 June onwards, I am concerned about the potential difficulties that delivery riders may face in meeting this requirement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not forget that a day a delivery rider does not have a competency certificate translates into a day without income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will provide them with some time to comply with this new requirement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill is clearly in the right direction in pivoting towards greater responsibility on the part of riders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it is not so clear with regard to the operative and substantive role played by platform companies in the safety and behaviour of their riders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Delivery riders are themselves also vulnerable road users.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They have a limited time to complete their job.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is not uncommon for them to take risks to avoid being penalised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This problem is worsened when riders are unaware of the road traffic rules.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These workers also do not enjoy the statutory benefits under the Work Injury Compensation Act, or WICA, in the event of an accident.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These companies might purchase third-party liability insurance now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, the compensation amount and protection under WICA is still superior.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that platform companies must take on greater responsibility in safeguarding the safety of both their riders and other road users.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Taking responsibility over the competency of the riders is the first step.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, section 47 imposes liability for allowing untested riders on the roads.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I would presume that these companies have liabilities because of their direct role in causing these untested riders to be on the road.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, if section 47K is intended to impose liability on platform companies, can the Ministry clarify whether the liability under section 47K attaches to the natural person who grants approval of the untested rider, or the company which the natural person is working for?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While I do note that section 2 of the Interpretation Act defines "person" to include a "company", it would be helpful for the Ministry to clarify on whom will the liability attach on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The incentive schemes and penalties embedded within the structures of the payouts directly contribute to road safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A platform company must know a route that a rider must take to deliver its assignment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It must then know the terrain and associated dangers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It must also know the number of hours that a rider has been on the job.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is clearly no different, for example, from a public transport operator knowing and being responsible for the hours worked by a bus captain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A review of the payout structures and time afforded for deliveries must be undertaken to align them with the new rules prescribed by the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, I suggest that the Ministry review the payout structures and deployment mechanism from a workplace and road safety perspective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would form part of the company's training efforts and its larger responsibility to other road users.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This should be the case whether a delivery rider can afford to pay for the test or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The underlying rationale behind this is for platform companies to be cognisant of their responsibility to these workers who are indispensable to their operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I propose for the Ministry, platform companies and the National Delivery Champions Association (NDCA) to work together to ensure the smooth administration of the theory test.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must bear in mind that some delivery riders might not be equipped to navigate these tests with ease.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I propose for the Ministry to ensure that the online tests are simple and comprehensible, while retaining the requisite substantive takeaways of the road traffic rules.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Like many of the other Members before me who have spoken on the need for vernacular languages, indeed, many of these riders, including the delivery riders, are senior and they may need some support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Additionally, I would like to suggest to the Ministry to establish an online database of every person who has been conferred a theory test certificate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the certificate being granted in digital form, it would be easier to unlawfully manipulate certificates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Platform companies play an important role in our economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding the above, I reiterate my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will speak on three key topics – cyclists, security searches and infrastructure for AVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The theory test will raise awareness on the rules and also, hopefully, serve as a reminder to experienced riders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share what are the costs involved to get certified to ride on the roads?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As some PAB users are riding for a livelihood, I think most of the Members have shared that the added expense could be a burden for them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the certifications be issued as physical cards or electronic digital certificates?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In designing the scheme, we must be wary of possible inequalities that may occur.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Official Handbook for Mandatory Theory Test released at the end of April for PABs and PMD scooters is quite comprehensive and useful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I tried to read all the pages in the handbook.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope it can be disseminated more extensively to our youths in schools as some aspects of the road traffic rules and practices are useful as well as for non-motorised bicycle users.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, as some Members have mentioned, a vernacular version of this handbook will be useful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can I ask if the relevant agencies' enforcement resources will be enhanced to meet the demands of these new amendments?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I now move on to security searches and checks, as mentioned in the Bill, which will be conducted on commuters as part of counter-terrorism efforts at our public transport nodes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I urge the authorities to ensure that the involved personnel are trained to conduct these searches as discreetly and as politely as possible.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We want to avoid issues of perceived, for example, racial profiling by the public, that can lead to further entrenchment of stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And as we are in the midst of a pandemic and body searches often require involved parties being at close proximity to each other, how can authorities guarantee the safety of the public and of the officers conducting the searches?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Looking ahead, I am pleased to note that the research and development trials for AVs are still going strong.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we open up new towns and estates and technology improves, it is inevitable that the usage of AVs will have future applications.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it is necessary to test the performance of self-driving software under real-world conditions, this should only happen after comprehensive safety testing and evaluation before we allow citizens to access the benefits of the technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Where will these trials and deployments take place and where can the public get access to regular updates?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The tragic incident has raised questions over self-driving technology: how safe is it and how much attention does it require from drivers?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some riders choose to make these trips on foot, some cycle, some get on their motorbikes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, getting around on power-assisted bicycles (PABs) are perceived by many riders as the most cost-effective and efficient way to make their deliveries.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Understandably, travelling on the roads, especially on PABs, poses its own set of dangers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Theory tests like this, beyond educating our riders about safe practices while travelling on roads, also delineate clearly what the responsibilities of riders are so that they may not be taken advantage of in disputes that occur on the roads, knowing what practices are well within their rights.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During the crisis, time and again, our delivery riders have proven themselves to be an essential service, bringing food to our families and keeping the food and beverage sector alive.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Simply put, they oil the gears of our society, especially at mealtimes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must ensure that these tests, essential as they are for awareness, education and safety, are inclusive and we cannot afford in any measure to allow these tests to become unfair barriers to the livelihood of our delivery riders in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, considering that the test will be online, delivery riders are also looking forward to the possibility that the fees for taking the test can be defrayed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the same vein, relating to the online nature of the tests, accessibility options must be provided for those who may find such online platforms challenging to navigate, or simply inaccessible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My residents often relate to me the conversations they have with other delivery riders about the best routes to take in the area, as well as the best makan spots along the way.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is the beauty of the delivery rider platform and community – that people from all walks of life can and do become delivery riders and are yet united by their shared livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To accommodate for this diversity, I think the theory test should account for literacy and language barriers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If possible, we would love to see a simply-worded test made available in multiple languages, with options, such as oral examinations, available even for those without basic literacy foundations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we understand that the tests may not be perpetually available for sitting to uphold the rigors of the standards, a day's delay for those who fail their test and who are unable to get on the road poses significant cost to the livelihoods of our delivery riders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The availability of these tests is also paramount to allow entry to becoming a delivery rider, as many delivery riders do this as a part-time gig, such as students on their holidays.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Having potentially to wait a week or two after applying to take the tests might set these prospective riders back unnecessarily.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All these being said, Mr Speaker, refining the administration of these theory tests is only half the story.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The education of our delivery riders can only elevate their prospects of safety so much.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this field of work, delivery platforms should place priority to the health, safety and lives of their partners.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is thus commendable that while we are enforcing the mandate of theory tests for riders on food delivery platforms, it is also essential that we try to secure the lives of our delivery riders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also be conscious that this goes hand in hand with securing their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Delivery riders who do not make their deliveries in a timely fashion according to the expectations of customers can accrue enough bad reviews to be penalised, if not banned.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we, on one hand, prescribe safe practices and speed limits in a test handbook and on the other hand have delivery riders fearing for their job security if they do not move fast enough?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Oftentimes, the delays in delivery times are not even the fault of riders but arise upstream, with the restaurants, though riders are well aware they are the ones who bear the brunt of these late deliveries, leading some to feel they have to make up for lost time and lost ground.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is so that we can safeguard the lives and livelihoods of our delivery riders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are clear ambitions to grow Singapore into a connected cycling-friendly city.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do not be surprised if we see cycling lanes on our roads one day, bicycle boulevards or even smart traffic lights that respond to the volume and type of vehicles on the road.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the push towards becoming a cycling-friendly city, the rules of the road and, naturally, the theory tests for PABs must be kept on their feet to change as our city also changes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When it comes to safety matters, we must be careful and not lose the big picture.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, these concerns not withstanding, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Since food has been delivered to the Members' Room, I propose to take a break now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.35 pm until 5.00 pm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, the Bill makes changes to the Road Traffic Act (RTA) to update our regulatory framework to facilitate trials of AVs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I am glad that many Members spoke up in support of this extension.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Singapore has been facilitating AV trials on public roads since 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Today, a growing eco-system of leading AV firms from China, Europe and the USA, such as Motional, Continental and Desay, have been conducting research and development (R&D) trials here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Local AV enterprises, such as ST Engineering Autonomous Solutions, have deployed on-demand commercial AV services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The sandbox will also support the large-scale pilot deployment of autonomous buses and shuttles that Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Melvin Yong asked about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This large-scale deployment will help us better understand the requirements for mass deployment, such as whether infrastructure upgrades are needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA will provide further updates in the lead up to deployment in the mid-2020s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The AV sandbox is meant to cover the trial and use of vehicles equipped with autonomous systems that enable the operation of vehicles without active physical control or monitoring by a human on public roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the use of the Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: ADAS technology requires active monitoring by human drivers and, therefore, does not fall within the realm of AV technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Before approving any motor vehicle for registration and use on public roads, including those fitted with ADAS, LTA checks to ensure the vehicle model’s compliance with stringent safety standards, such as those set out by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) and the Vehicle Construction and Use Rules under the RTA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As ADAS technology grows more advanced, we agree with Mr Melvin Yong’s observation that it may carry new risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are monitoring global developments closely and will consider further regulation if necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides the sandbox, another move LTA made to support AV trials was to expand the AV testbed in 2019 to include 1,000 kilometres of public roads in western Singapore, covering a wide range of traffic scenarios and road conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This has served the needs of AV developers interested to deploy AVs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, there are developers who may be considering other environments for their trials beyond western Singapore, as suggested by Ms Poh Li San, and LTA is open to such considerations when assessing their trial applications on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In trialling AVs, public safety is our top priority.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is why LTA has put in place stringent safety assessments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat will be pleased to know that there are milestone tests in place today, administered in a specially-designed facility – the Centre of Excellence for Testing and Research of AVs at NTU, or CETRAN.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: All AVs must undergo and pass these tests prior to on-road trials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: All AVs must also have a qualified safety driver onboard who can take immediate control of the vehicle during trials, should the need arise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These safety drivers are subject to the same responsibility as drivers of manned vehicles in ensuring the safe driving of the vehicle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The requirement for safety drivers will remain in place until AVs are able to operate safely without a human driver.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We agree with Ms Poh Li San’s observation that the liability and insurance framework for AVs is just as important as the underlying technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is why all AV developers, as owners of the AVs, are legally required to purchase third-party liability insurance for all AV trials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In the event of an accident, the insurance will cover any losses or damages that the owner and any authorised safety driver may suffer, as a result of any injury, death and property damage caused to any third party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is not much different from the motor insurance coverage for manned vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: All AVs must also carry data recorders to collect data to support investigations in case of incidents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But as we move towards fully autonomous transport in the longer term, MOT and LTA will need to adapt and review the liability framework for motor vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Among other things, we are working with legal experts and insurers to better understand how to ascertain and assign liability in the case of accidents involving autonomous driving systems, as suggested by Ms Poh Li San.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While there are potential benefits, Ms Poh Li San has also rightly pointed out that AV technology can be disruptive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will pace the transition carefully so that livelihoods will not be severely disrupted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will ensure that public bus captains are equipped with the necessary skills for new job roles, to continue contributing to the public transport system even when autonomous buses are introduced into the public transport fleet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For taxi and private hire car drivers, LTA will be updating the vocational licence training curriculum after engaging the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The new curriculum will keep drivers up to date on new technologies, such as AVs and digitalisation, in the future economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA will be seeking feedback from the industry, as well as the National Taxi Association and the National Private Hire Vehicles’ Association, before finalising the new curriculum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, the Bill will update and future-proof our vehicular tax system, which is a key part of our vehicular controls and management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: All vehicles used or kept in Singapore are subject to taxes upon registration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, ambulances and fire engines are exempted as they provide essential public services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, when these vehicles are no longer on a tax-exempt scheme, it is only fair to all other vehicle owners and drivers that taxes are re-imposed on these vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: MOH has announced enhanced regulatory standards for private ambulances and medical transporters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are amending the RTA today, as shown in clauses 6 to 8 of the Bill, to facilitate and clarify LTA’s existing practices and to streamline the existing legislative provisions related to tax re-imposition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At the same time, we will amend the RTA, via clauses 4 and 5 of the Bill, to facilitate the recovery of undercharged or under-declared taxes as fines, similar to the existing provision for the Government to recover road tax arrears.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Third, the Bill will make changes that help ensure our public transport system remains safe and secure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clauses 24 and 31 of the Bill empower the Police and authorised officers to carry out security searches on persons on the public transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Considering that the public transport system plays a critical role in Singapore, we need to remain vigilant and safeguard it against such threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Members asked for the authorised officers to be appropriately trained to ensure security searches are conducted professionally, as well as in a discreet and polite manner without entrenching stereotypes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These security searches are conducted similar to those carried out at major events, such as at the National Day Parade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In their training, the authorised officers are taught how to spot anyone displaying suspicious behaviour without bias against any race or religion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Only upon completion of the training and certification can they be considered as "Senior Approved Persons" as defined in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
