text: Members asked about the types of measures that would be applied during frisk searches to prevent passengers from being taken advantage of.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition, security searches will be conducted within the video surveillance coverage to provide assurance to the public that any alleged abuses will be investigated accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also have the powers to enforce against imposters, as provided for under section 11B of the LTA Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked how we will ensure the safety of the public and authorised officers, especially during the current COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Adequate safe management measures have been put in place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Authorised officers are required to strictly adhere to these measures as well as the MOH’s health advisory.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The authorised officers are also reminded to practise good personal hygiene.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: All security equipment is regularly sanitised after each use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition, hand sanitisers will be provided for commuters to use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I will now address the broader land transport issues raised by Members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: With regard to illegal modifications, it is already an offence for any person to illegally modify a vehicle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They can be fined up to $5,000 and/or jailed up to three months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Like Mr Derrick Goh suggested, vehicular inspections are a key touchpoint during which illegal modifications can be detected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We introduced the Enhanced Inspection Regime where vehicle owners caught with illegally modified exhaust systems for a second or subsequent time will be subjected to more frequent mandatory vehicle inspections.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I shared with this House in March about the challenges of enforcing against errant motor workshops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: That said, we have stepped up enforcements island-wide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Just last week, a motor vehicle workshop was charged in Court for illegally modifying two cars’ exhaust systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is a very serious offence, as modifying a vehicle's exhaust system may lead to public safety concerns when the vehicle is used for racing, or result in public nuisance due to excessive noise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Vehicle safety is a key concern and we will do more to deter illegal modifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To this effect, we will strengthen penalties for illegal exhaust modifications for greater deterrence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For first-time offenders, LTA currently issues a composition sum of $500.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also not hesitate to take offenders of more egregious cases to Court, even if they are first-time offenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I am glad that many Members have voiced their support for the theory test for e-scooters and power-assisted bicycle (PAB) riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is not a licensing regime which will be more onerous for riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Instead, it is a one-time theory test which will ensure that riders are familiar with active mobility rules, regulations and code of conduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To answer Ms He Ting Ru's query, the minimum riding age for PAB and e-scooters is 16 and riders will be required to take and pass the test before being able to ride.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: E-scooter riders below the age of 16 can only ride under adult supervision and the supervising adult will need to have passed the test.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA just launched the English handbook for e-scooter and PAB riders and we will make available the Mandarin, Malay and Tamil translations shortly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The handbook is available free-of-charge and we will study suggestions raised by Members on more widely disseminating the information, including through schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To address Mr Gan Thiam Poh's question, the handbook includes information on what to do in an accident, on top of rules and code of conduct and a section on equipment check.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: On Mr Darryl David's question on including a practical component, the theory test is a useful start to address the lack of knowledge of rules and to tackle deliberate errant riding behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will continue to monitor the landscape and update the testing requirements, if necessary, while balancing against how onerous the regime will be on PAB riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA will release more details in June, but I will address some key points, such as the cost of the test and if it will be accessible to those who face difficulty taking an online test, including our seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will keep test fees affordable to minimise the financial impact on riders, especially those who ride for their livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: And just in case Members do not really understand what it means, let me just clarify.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Five dollars for two attempts means if you try the first time, it will be $5.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: If you pass, we are happy for you.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: If you cannot pass, you can take the test again for free the second time; that is, $5 for two attempts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is a discounted rate to encourage greater test take-up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The test will be conducted online in the four official languages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Special provisions can be made on a case-by-case basis for those who are not digitally-savvy or illiterate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Upon passing, digital certificates will be issued to the rider.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will have the means to verify unlawful manipulation of the certificate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will provide an adequate transition period for riders to prepare, take and complete the test before enforcement kicks in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will work through the NTUC, food delivery companies and active mobility interest groups to raise awareness and ensure that all riders are certified before they ride.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I am glad to hear from Mr Abdul Samad that the NTUC is working on a training programme to prepare delivery riders for the test.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked if the new section 47K also imposes liability on platform companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To Mr Gan Thiam Poh's and Mr Derrick Goh's queries on errant riders caught flouting traffic regulations, they are already required to undergo the Safe Riding Programme, which includes both theory and practical components today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: On enforcement, Mr Saktiandi Supaat's and Mr Gan Thiam Poh's suggestion of using technology is a good one.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA's MyTransport.SG mobile application has a "snap and send" function that enables members of the public to report errant riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA is also trialling using CCTV technology and video analytics to identify errant riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Darryl David, Dr Shahira Abdullah, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Sharael Taha have also asked about the safe use of bicycles on our roads and paths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This has been an on-going effort and one which LTA has devoted much attention and resources to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Over the years, we have put in place a regulatory framework to provide clarity on rules, launched outreach and public education programmes and enhanced our enforcement efforts against errant riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat spoke about this at length, including how we are expanding the active mobility infrastructure, which Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Raeesah Khan have suggested.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have recently asked Active Mobility Advisory Panel or AMAP to conduct a review to improve road safety for both cyclists and motorists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Among other issues, AMAP will study how to enhance public education and awareness of rules for all road users – both cyclists and motorists alike.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: AMAP will engage different stakeholders and submit their recommendations in due course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At the same time, we will press on with enforcement against errant riders and motorists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: That said, I would like to point out to Mr Dennis Tan that road safety has to be a collective effort from all road users to play their part by driving and riding safely, to be considerate to one another and to do their part to build up a safe riding culture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Murali Pillai, Ms Hazel Poa, Ms He Ting Ru and Dr Shahira Abdullah have asked about enhancing the safety of using lorries to ferry workers and provided many suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This issue is not within the ambit of the Bill and has already been addressed extensively yesterday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I will not deal with this in detail again.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Internationally, practices involving the use of lorries to ferry workers are varied and we have studied this widely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While some Members have identified countries that disallow the practice, there are also countries, such as Canada, Thailand and the USA, that allow workers to be ferried in the rear deck of lorries, albeit with safety precautions and some restrictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is an important point to note and it shows that this practice is not uncommon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: There are also very significant, practical and operational issues, as I have noted, on top of just cost considerations that need to be considered in any enhancements of existing measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These are not vague statements, but concrete feedback given by many companies and SMEs, and reflect the realities on the ground.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Such moves will have wider ramifications, including on livelihoods for both local and migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: If the Member who raised this, Ms He Ting Ru, speaks to SMEs on the ground, I am sure she would know this even without having to do a study.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: So, while it is clearly not just about cost, to argue as though cost does not matter at all, is not practical and does not gel with reality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: What we have been striving to do is to preserve the safety of workers and, at the same time, ensure that they can continue to have their jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In the meantime, we will continue engaging employers and drivers of lorries to remind them about our rules and encourage safe driving behaviours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also step up enforcement against any non-compliance with regulatory requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: And we urge all employers to do their part in ensuring the safety and welfare of their drivers and workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In sum, MOT will continue with our efforts to make Singapore's land transport system more future-ready, resilient and safe.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This Bill is part of that work and I thank Members for their support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The first question is I wonder if the Senior Minister of State could explain to us regarding frisk searches whether commuters can expect these searches to be targeted, that is, based on suspicion, or would they also be conducted on a random basis, as a general deterrent to would-be offenders?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, that is the first question – whether it is targeted or does it also include random searches for no suspicion at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second question is, she mentioned that the persons who would be empowered to do frisk searches and other searches would receive the relevant training in consultation with MHA and she highlighted that they would have to undergo WSQ courses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Would she be able to tell us which modules they would be required to undergo?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And, lastly, I heard what she said about the safeguards for searching of passengers, including searching of women to be done by only women personnel, as well as the searches to be done in a video recorded area.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Because there are different threat levels and, depending on the threat levels, they will be doing their checks at the public transport areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Regarding informing the public, awareness by public, well, I am sure this is recorded, this will be publicised.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also look at how we can ensure and reach out to the public further, in order to make sure that the public also know and have assurance that this is done.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But having said that, it is really not just about the public knowing it because our authorised officers have a duty, responsibility and obligation to ensure that they do this in accordance with protocols and SOPs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Murali Pillai, you have got a quick clarification?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One, the hon Senior Minister of State mentioned that I had, in my speech, spoken about migrant workers being transported in lorries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would just like to clarify that I did not do so in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Second one, again, a short point of clarification, Senior Minister of State Amy Khor mentioned about the point that I raised in my speech which refers to the fact that there is no offence linking an owner of a vehicle who was lackadaisical in maintaining his vehicle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The point I actually made was a bit different.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I recognise that there are provisions in that regard, but my point was a bit more involved.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I was talking about a case where an owner is lackadaisical in maintaining his vehicles which led to a fatal accident or injuries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That is the point I was making but I do not need any response from the learned Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor has addressed the questions relating to areas under MOT’s purview.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will now address those under MHA’s purview.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: First, on MHA’s proposals to raise penalties for offences relating to illegal speed trials, helmets, individuals who obstruct, prevent or defeat the course of justice, and road rage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Second, on MHA’s proposals to enhance TP’s operational efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: First, let me address Members’ questions on the raising of penalties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: A non-mandatory forfeiture regime does not mean that offenders get off easy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The burden of proof is on the owner to prove, to the satisfaction of the Court, that the vehicle was used without his consent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In such situations, we can let the Court decide, by looking at all the facts of the case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This also ensures parity with forfeiture for other offences in the RTA and in other Acts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This House would recall that in 2019, we amended the RTA to provide for non-mandatory forfeiture of vehicles involved in the offence of dangerous and careless driving.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As another example, under the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA), if a person is convicted of any offence and if the Public Prosecutor makes an application to forfeit a vehicle, the Court shall order the vehicle to be forfeited unless the owner establishes that the vehicle was unlawfully in the possession of another person without the owner’s consent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked about the situation where the owner was wilfully blind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In other words, the owner suspected that his car could be used in an illegal speed trial, but did not ask.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As I have mentioned earlier, the burden is on the owner to prove to the satisfaction of the Court that the vehicle had been used without his consent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In a case where the owner suspected that the offender used his vehicle and could have asked, but did not, it is up to the Court to decide, based on the facts of the case, whether there had been implied consent to the use of the vehicle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If the Court finds that there was implied consent, the vehicle will be forfeited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked how we would be able to discern genuine cases of owners claiming that they did not provide consent to the offending drivers to use their vehicles in illegal speed trials.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As part of the investigative process, TP interviews all involved parties separately and procures other relevant evidence, such as video footage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This evidence will be submitted to the Court, for the Court to decide based on the facts of the case and the arguments from both sides.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For non-genuine cases, TP will not hesitate to take action against the persons or anyone who falsely claimed that the offending driver had used the vehicle without the owner’s consent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They may be charged for the offence of providing false or misleading information and face a jail term, a fine, or both, if found guilty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked if TP will step up enforcement to increase detection of illegal speed trials.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: TP will continue to monitor the road safety situation and assess if there is a need to install more enforcement cameras.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: TP will also continue to conduct regular enforcement operations at known hotspots and will mount additional enforcement operations where necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Regarding the minimum age for child pillion riders, Mr Murali Pillai is correct that the minimum age for pillion riders on motorcycles is 10, while the minimum age for pillion riders on PABs is higher, at 16.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Motorcyclists, unlike PAB riders, go through more stringent training and testing before they are allowed to ride their vehicle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As part of the process to obtain a driving licence, motorcyclists will need to take two theory tests, go through a series of riding lessons, before taking their practical test.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The training includes a module on how to ride safely with a pillion rider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On the other hand, PAB riders only need to go through a theory test and do not need to undergo any practical test.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The motorcyclist has, therefore, undergone more training and is better able to handle a motorcycle with a pillion rider compared to the PAB rider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We are conscious of the costs of getting helmets certified, a point raised by Mr Sharael Taha.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Singapore Motor Cycle Trade Association has also raised this concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The current standards used to certify motorcycle helmets was formulated in 2014, in consultation with the industry and technical experts, including the Singapore Motor Cycle Trade Association.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These are in line with the internationally recognised United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Regulation Number 22, though we have additional requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, Singapore’s previous review concluded that it is important to include additional tests, such as the penetration test, which tests how easily the helmet’s shell is penetrated when it hits a sharp object, such as a fence or a motorcycle footrest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: That said, we hear the concerns about the costs of certification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have to balance against the safety of road users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will work with the relevant stakeholders to find the right balance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Enforcement and penalties are not enough to ensure road safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: TP will also conduct more public education on the importance of wearing proper helmets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As Ms Joan Pereira pointed out, there are risks in wearing a helmet that does not meet regulatory requirements or is not of the right size.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Next, on individuals who obstruct, prevent or defeat the course of justice, Ms Sylvia Lim asked why we are increasing the penalties for the offence of furnishing false particulars to TP, especially since we had only done so recently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked what the penalties are for a cyclist exhibiting road rage to a motorist and whether we can ensure that there are equal consequences for cyclists and motorists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The RTA provides that if a motorist commits an offence, such as voluntarily causing hurt while being a driver of a motor vehicle, he is liable for an additional offence of "road rage" and the Court may make an order to disqualify the offender from driving, or holding or obtaining a driving licence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This disqualification is on top of the penalties that the motorist may face for the underlying offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The policy intent of this provision is to prevent motorists who have committed road rage from driving a motor vehicle again, as the behaviour might be repeated and cause harm to other motorists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The penalty of disqualification is, therefore, only applicable to motorists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In the scenario painted by the Member, where the cyclist verbally abuses and punches a motorist, the Court may not disqualify the cyclist from driving.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The cyclist's behaviour may not represent his driving behaviour since he was not driving a motor vehicle at the time of the offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It may not be possible for the Judge to assess whether it is undesirable for the cyclist to be allowed to drive a motor vehicle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Nonetheless, the cyclist will still be liable for the relevant underlying penalty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the logic of making the chairperson, managing director or company secretary of a company responsible for maintaining a proper record of the vehicle's usage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He suggested that we can instead require that the Board appoints an employee to be the responsible person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The responsibilities of the chairperson, managing director or company secretary would then be discharged once the appointment is made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To clarify, this provision does not require the chairperson, managing director or company secretary to actually carry out the record keeping personally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Instead, they are to ensure the keeping of such records.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ensuring that records are properly kept so that investigations into a traffic incident can be conducted promptly is very important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We want the company to take this seriously and actively take steps towards this end, by designating its chairman, managing director or company secretary, or any position analogous to these offices, to be responsible for ensuring that records are properly kept.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if we would be enhancing enforcement efforts to complement the new offences to deter irresponsible driving behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Over the years, TP has enhanced its enforcement strategy by leveraging technology to improve detection of offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: TP has also become more transparent with motorists by alerting them before they reach enforcement camera zones, to encourage them to drive more safely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: TP will also enforce against motorists who commit the new offences as part of their existing enforcement strategy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali Pillai shared his views that we should hold vehicle owners and operators of vehicles criminally liable for fatal and injury-causing accidents which are due to mechanical failure in the vehicle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I agree that it is important that vehicles are well maintained, to ensure the safety of not just the occupants but other road users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is why for accidents involving mechanical failure, such as when the vehicle's brakes are faulty, TP can already take to task the person who holds the responsibility to maintain the vehicle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: That said, we hear the Member's suggestion and we will work with MOT to review how we can strengthen this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked MHA to consider allowing individuals with financial difficulties to pay road traffic fines in instalments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As mentioned in MHA's Committee of Supply debate in 2021, MHA has been studying this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There are several considerations that MHA will have to think through.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: First, whether instalment plans would dilute the deterrent effect of the fines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While we empathise with those facing financial difficulties, we also have a duty to ensure the safety of all other road users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Second, resources that could otherwise have been used to directly enhance road safety, will have to be diverted to monitor instalment plans and manage appeals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These details would have to be worked through.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If I may quote Mr Murali Pillai, he said, "It is clear that legislation must not be the only policy instrument to protect our most vulnerable on the roads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As Ms Joan Pereira highlighted, public engagement and education on our road traffic rules are important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In this regard, TP and LTA have been continuously working with various stakeholders to improve road safety.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I have a clarification for the Minister of State.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We work with our stakeholders, as I have shared earlier, to improve road safety for the motorcyclists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For education, for example, since December 2020, we have a new feature as part of the education process for learner motorcyclists, where we introduced simulation training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They have to go through a few modules, where they will be able to identify and go through the process of top 10 vulnerable accident-prone situations in the simulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We also have a riding theory handbook available online for them to learn.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we continuously engage motorcyclists because we know they are a vulnerable group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In the last few months when I was involved, I went around in a TP car to identify riders who practised safe habits, such as wearing the necessary gear well and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I think that actually spread among the motorcyclist community and it gave a very positive vibe and message to motorcyclists that it is good to be on the safe side, to practise good habits for road safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As I have mentioned earlier, we will continue to enforce where we work with community partners; we work with the feedback that we receive and look at the hotspots where there may be opportunities for us, not only to enforce, but also to educate, engage and bring out positive impact, not only to the motorcyclist community, but for all road users as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: First of all, I would like to thank her for highlighting that PAB users taking the test do not have to pay for the second round of test.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But I would like to ask a question with regard to the audio version of the test.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I found out that for some places in Australia, in New South Wales, the transport agency creates a hotline for those taking the road theory test and for those who have learning difficulties or special needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, is there a possibility that we can create an audio version of the test?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And second, whether we can create a hotline for PAB users who have learning difficulties, for example, those who have trouble reading or understanding questions for them to make arrangements in that regard?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Just let me say that it is free only for the repeat test taken in first three months.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But having said that, as I said, we are mindful to make sure it is affordable to PAB riders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the Member's suggestion for an audio version of the test, first, let me say that, on a case-by-case basis, there is a need for special consideration, they can actually do an oral test.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But I think his idea of an audio version, meaning an online audio version, is a good idea.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We can look into this and study to see if it is feasible.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the hotline, they can contact LTA and let them know if there are special requests.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have a clarification for Minister of State Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Earlier he mentioned that nationwide, we have about 300 cameras to detect speeding offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I do note that it is more than before.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But from time to time, we also get requests from residents for us to convey to TP that they would like speed cameras installed at certain locations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The reply from TP, typically, is that they would consider the matter and any decision whether or not to install would depend on the accident rate as well as public feedback.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I would like him to confirm that TP does not need accidents to happen before they decide whether to install a camera at a certain location.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I am not sure whether the Member was in the House when I answered a similar question on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: TP does not wait for traffic accidents to happen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Essentially, we work with various stakeholders and when we have feedback that there is a certain hotspot, or even, not a hotspot, but feedback relating to speeding in certain areas, we will go down and take a look.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: When we go down, it does not mean that we will install a camera in the area.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: But we will do our intelligence work and enforcement operations around the area, making sure that even before we install a camera, we know that there is a real problem there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If there are other solutions, we will continue with other alternatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I want to assure the Member that we do not wait for traffic accidents to happen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is something that we all know very well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is the operational procedure of what we do at TP.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: He earlier mentioned about statistics where over the last 10 years till 2019, traffic fatalities have dropped.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: However, in that lower number, about 80% of traffic fatalities relate to the elderly.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: So, the clarification question for the Minister of State is whether there are plans and initiatives that have been put in place to address this given that our population is ageing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In addition to that, we also engage the senior community by working with Senior Activity Centres and Lion Befrienders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Just in February this year, TP launched the Eye Care Kit to work with the seniors on how they are able to walk and travel safely.
